Because it travels with each event, a tab holding a stale copy of `GET /api/notifications/config` still honours the current policy.

**`pushed`** is `true` when this notification is also being delivered over Web Push to this user; a client holding an active push subscription may skip its own OS toast because the service worker will show one. It is independent of `toast`.

post.description:
The only recall mechanism this feature has. Accepted for a `scheduled`, `sending` or `failed` broadcast and refused with 409 for any other status (`sent`, `canceled`). Applied as a conditional write, so it races the fan-out's own claim — and the flip to `failed` when a fan-out job gives up — inside the database where exactly one of them can win. Cancelling a `failed` broadcast is how an operator who will not resume it closes the record.

⚠ CANCELLING A BROADCAST THAT IS ALREADY `sending` MAY STILL LET ONE IN-FLIGHT BATCH GO OUT: the fan-out re-checks the status between batches, so up to one chunk's worth of recipients (BROADCAST_CHUNK_SIZE, currently 200) can already have been dispatched or be mid-dispatch when the cancel lands. Cancel stops everything after that point; it cannot recall what has already been sent.

The row is kept, not deleted — a pulled announcement is exactly what an operator needs to look up later. Queued job rows are also left alone: deleting them would race a worker claiming one, the handlers' status checks are the durable gate, and the rows are the audit history of what the fan-out actually did.

**Requires:** authentication, plus at least one of the permissions `broadcasts:write` or `org_broadcasts:write`.

Continues a `failed` broadcast from where its fan-out stopped. A broadcast becomes `failed` when one of its fan-out jobs gives up permanently (its attempt or rate-limit budget is spent); `lastError` says which job and why. REPLACES THE PRODUCTION DATABASE. Requires `db_backup:restore`, which is a SEPARATE permission from `db_backup:write` precisely so it can be withheld from someone who may schedule backups but must not be able to replace the database.

The body must be exactly `{"confirmation":"RESTORE"}` (plus an optional `overrideSchemaCheck`). The literal is the safety feature: a retried, replayed or mis-fired POST cannot reconstruct it by accident, and a missing or wrong confirmation is a `400` that starts NOTHING — no pre-flight, no download, no row.

Returns as soon as the cheap pre-flight gates have run. ⚠ READ `mode`, NOT ONLY THE STATUS CODE: all three normal outcomes are `200`.

`running` — the gates passed and the restore is under way in the background. It takes HOURS (every index is rebuilt from the archive), so poll `GET runs/{id}` and watch `restoreStatus`: `restoring` → `verifying` → `swapping` → `completed`/`failed`. The application serves normally throughout; the only destructive window is two catalog renames long, and the process exits at the end of it so its connection pool can be rebuilt — a restart policy is a hard prerequisite.

`guided` — a CAPABILITY gate failed (typically the role lacks `CREATEDB`, which managed PostgreSQL routinely denies). Nothing was started. This is NOT an error: the body carries a complete, paste-ready command block with real names, hosts and ports, plus a runbook path, so the same restore can be performed by hand with a superuser.

`blocked` — the schema-compatibility gate refused. Nothing was started. Compare `preflight.archiveMigration` with `preflight.liveMigration` and, if you accept the mismatch, re-send with `overrideSchemaCheck: true`. ⚠ That flag unblocks THAT GATE AND NOTHING ELSE — it can never bypass a capability gate, because no amount of accepting makes a role without `CREATEDB` able to create a database.

`preflight.gates` lists EVERY gate that ran, including the ones that passed, so an operator can see what was checked rather than only what failed.

Reports this deployment: the API version the process resolved for itself, the deploy document `appctl deploy` left on disk, and a database liveness fact.

**Always answers `200`.** A missing document is `deployInfoStatus: "absent"`, an unreadable or malformed one is `"invalid"`, and a database that does not answer is `database: null` with a `databaseError` string. None of the three is an error status: this endpoint is read when something has gone wrong, so every failure it can have is a field rather than a status code.

**Three deploy states, not two.** Beyond `ok` and `absent`, a document can be complete AND describe a run that failed — `deployInfoStatus: "ok"` with `run.outcome: "failure"` and `run.failedStep` naming where it stopped. That run still deployed something, so every fact it recorded is reported.

`deployInfoPath` is the exact path that was read, and on an `absent` answer it is the actionable fact — the file may simply be at a different path, on an unattached bind mount, or from a run that stopped before writing it.

info.title: Hexactra Console API
info.description:
The HTTP API behind the **Hexactra Console** — a production-grade application
base with Google OAuth sign-in, role- and permission-based authorization, per-user and
system settings, object storage, and an email allowlist gating who may sign in at all.

This page is generated from the running server (build `0.0.0`), so it always matches the
deployment you are pointed at. The machine-readable document is at
[`/api/openapi.json`](/api/openapi.json).

---

## Getting a token

Authentication is applied per route. Every operation below states which credentials it
accepts; an operation with no security requirement listed needs none (the health probes and
the sign-in routes themselves).

There are three ways to obtain a bearer token, in rough order of how often you will want each.

### 1. Your browser session (fastest, for exploring these docs)

If you are already signed in to this deployment in this browser, press **Authorize with my
session** at the top of this page. It calls `POST /api/auth/refresh` with your existing refresh
cookie and loads the returned access token into the client below. Nothing to copy or paste, and
the authorization survives a reload.

Access tokens are short-lived (15 minutes by default). If calls start returning `401`, press the
button again.

### 2. Personal access token — scripts and automation

Mint a `pat_…` token via `POST /api/pat` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer pat_…`. The
authentication guard recognizes the `pat_` prefix before it ever reaches JWT verification, so a
PAT is accepted on **every** authenticated route in this document — there is no narrower scope.
It resolves to the full role and permission set of the user that minted it, which is why it should
be treated exactly like that user's password. Revoke with `DELETE /api/pat/{id}`.

### 3. Device authorization grant — CLI and other browserless clients

For a machine that cannot open a browser, use the RFC 8628 flow: `POST /api/auth/device/code`
to get a user code, show it to the user, and poll `POST /api/auth/device/token` until they
approve it at the activation page. Sessions created this way are listed and revocable under
**Device Authorization**; revoking one also revokes the credential the device collected.

Note that sign-in of any kind is gated by the email allowlist: an address an administrator has
not added cannot complete OAuth at all, regardless of which flow it uses.

---

## Response shape

A global response interceptor wraps every successful JSON body in a `data` envelope, adding a
sibling `meta` carrying the server timestamp:

```json
{
  "data": { "id": "…", "email": "…" },
  "meta": { "timestamp": "2026-08-17T04:37:58.000Z" }
}
```

The one exception is a handler that already returns an object with a `data` key — the interceptor
passes those through untouched, so they get no `meta`. The response schema shown for each
operation is authoritative; it is generated by applying that same rule to the document.

### Paginated lists

Every list endpoint is offset-paginated with `page` and `pageSize` query parameters, but there
are **two different body shapes**, and a client that consumes more than one list will hit both:

- **Flat** — `GET /api/users`, `GET /api/allowlist`. Counts sit beside `items`:

  ```json
  { "data": { "items": [ … ], "total": 42, "page": 1, "pageSize": 20, "totalPages": 3 } }
  ```

- **Nested** — `GET /api/storage/objects`. Counts sit in a `meta` object *inside* `data`, and
  the total is named `totalItems` rather than `total`:

  ```json
  { "data": { "items": [ … ], "meta": { "page": 1, "pageSize": 20, "totalItems": 42, "totalPages": 3 } } }
  ```

Note also that the inner `meta` of a nested list is a different object from the envelope's own
`meta`, which holds the timestamp. This asymmetry is a known defect, tracked separately; it is
documented here rather than quietly smoothed over because the wire format is what it is today and
a client has to handle both.

---

## Errors

Every error passes through one exception filter, which rebuilds the body from a fixed key
allowlist. These six keys are the complete set — nothing else can appear:

```json
{
  "statusCode": 409,
  "code": "CONFLICT",
  "message": "Email already in allowlist",
  "details": { "field": "email" },
  "timestamp": "2026-08-17T04:37:58.000Z",
  "path": "/api/allowlist"
}
```

`details` is present only when the failure carried structured data, and it is the **only** place
endpoint-specific data survives: a custom top-level field on a thrown exception is dropped before
it reaches you. `code` is derived from the status by the filter and overrides anything the thrown
exception set, so it is always one of the values enumerated on `ErrorDto` — branch on it rather
than on `message`, which is prose.

Errors are **not** wrapped in the `data` envelope: the filter writes straight to the reply and
bypasses the response interceptor.

---

## Permissions

Authorization is a single layer. A user holds one or more **system roles** — `admin`,
`contributor`, `viewer` — and each role grants a set of **permissions** named `resource:action`
(`users:read`, `system_settings:write`, `storage:delete_any`, `rbac:manage`).

Guarded operations state their requirements in a generated **Requires:** line. Where several
roles are listed the guard admits any one of them; where several permissions are listed the guard
requires all of them. Those lines are rendered from the same `@Auth()` metadata the guards read,
so they cannot drift from what the server enforces.

Deactivated users are rejected at authentication time regardless of their roles.

---

## Conventions

- All timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
- All ids are UUIDs unless documented otherwise.
- Object sizes are returned as **strings**, not numbers — they are 64-bit values that would lose
  precision as JSON numbers.
- `204 No Content` responses have no body, and are therefore not enveloped.
- The API is served same-origin under `/api`; this document's server is `/`.

## Further reading

Architecture, security and operations documentation lives in the repository under
[`docs/`](https://github.com/marinoscar/hexactra/tree/main/docs).

anyOf.description: The agent policy a run runs under; null until the run has started.

stopReason.description: Why the run stopped (typed): finished, budget_* (actions, model_calls, active_time, input_tokens, output_tokens, cost), stalled, cancelled, error or no_model. Null while it runs and on runs from before this field.

effective.description: The limits the run is held to, fixed at its start: the policy budget clamped by the deployment ceilings. `null` is unlimited. Active time is in minutes, cost in USD.

used.description: What the run has used so far, in the same units (active time includes the stretch in progress).

percent.description: Percent of each limit used, one decimal; `null` for an unlimited budget.

source.description: Where each limit came from: the `policy`, or the deployment `ceiling` that clamped it. `null` when unlimited.

costKnown.description: False when a call could not be priced: `used.cost` is then "at least".

anyOf.description: The run budget: `null` on a run that has not started or that was snapshotted before budgets were enforced.

start.description: The tier the policy starts runs on

max.description: The highest tier the run may escalate to

current.description: The tier the run is on now: the start tier until a stall escalates it

escalations.description: How many times the run escalated

model.description: The current tier's model, as `provider:modelId`; null when none was resolved

anyOf.description: The run's model tier, from its policy snapshot: null until the run has started.

currentTier.description: The model tier the run is on now. It moves up when the run stalls and back down after progress. Null before the run starts.

escalations.description: How many times the run moved to a stronger tier because it stalled

cachedInputTokens.description: Input tokens the provider served from its cache (part of inputTokens)

modelCalls.description: Model calls (provider round trips) made so far

costUsd.description: USD spent on model calls, from the admin price table (agentPricing); a lower bound while costKnown is false

costKnown.description: False once a call could not be priced because its model has no price: show costUsd as "at least"

valueWithheld.description: True for a secret: the value went to the browser, single use, and is never returned

policyId.description: Run under this agent policy for this run only ("Run with..."), instead of the schedule's, the task's or the user's default.
Run under this agent policy instead of the task's or the user's default.
Overrides the task's agent policy for scheduled runs; null follows the task

description.description: The expression in words (English, 24-hour), e.g. "Monday to Friday at 09:00"

timezone.description: The zone a schedule gets when its request names none

source.description: `profile`: the user's profile time zone. `device`: the profile follows the device and the request carried `X-Time-Zone`. `default`: neither, so UTC.

valid.description: True: `cron`, `timezone`, `description`, `next` and `intervalSeconds` are present. False: `code` and `message` are.

timezone.description: The zone the firings were computed in: the one sent, or the default

description.description: The expression in words (English, 24-hour), e.g. "Monday to Friday at 09:00"

intervalSeconds.description: Seconds between firings when the next ones are evenly spaced; null for an uneven schedule (week days, days of the month, a daylight-saving change)

code.description: Why the schedule would be refused

timezone.description: Omitted: the owner's profile time zone.
